---
title: "Quiz: self-distillation and foundation models"
---

Short questions on students, teachers, collapse and frozen features. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

---

**Q1.** In self-distillation, which network is trained by backpropagation, and how does the other one change?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
One of them gets no gradient.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The student is trained by backpropagation to match the teacher's output on another view. The teacher gets no gradient; its weights are a moving average of the student's weights, updated after every step.
:::

---

**Q2.** Self-distillation has no negatives. What stops every image from getting the same output?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Two operations on the teacher's output.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Centring (subtracting a running mean of the teacher's scores) stops one prototype from winning for all images; sharpening (a low teacher temperature) stops the outputs from becoming uniform. Together, with the slowly moving teacher, they keep the outputs confident per image and different between images.
:::

---

**Q3.** With $m = 0.99$, how far has the teacher followed a sudden change of the student after 100 steps?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$1 - m^n$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$1 - 0.99^{100} = 0.63$: about two thirds.
:::

---

**Q4.** Name two ways in which microscopy images differ from the photographs most foundation models were trained on.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Channels, scale, what texture means.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
For example: many fluorescence channels instead of three colours; objects of a few pixels in very large fields; texture that carries biological meaning (chromatin) rather than surface; no natural orientation; intensities that are measurements.
:::

---

**Q5.** You cluster frozen embeddings of cells from 12 plates and get 12 clean clusters. What do you check before calling them phenotypes?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Colour the clusters by something technical.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Whether the clusters coincide with the plates (a batch effect). If so, centre the embeddings per plate using control cells and cluster again; and evaluate on held-out plates.
:::

---

**Q6.** How does an image–text model classify an image into classes it was never trained on?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Both images and captions are embedded in the same space.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Embed each class name as a caption ("a nucleus in mitosis", …), embed the image, and choose the caption with the most similar embedding (zero-shot). It only works for concepts described in its training captions.
:::

---

**Q7.** *(math)* Show that the gradient of $-\sum_k t_k\ln s_k$ with $s = \mathrm{softmax}(\mathbf g/\tau)$ with respect to $\mathbf g$ is $(s - t)/\tau$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Write $\ln s_k = g_k/\tau - \ln\sum_j e^{g_j/\tau}$ and use $\sum_k t_k = 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The loss is $-\sum_k t_k g_k/\tau + \ln\sum_j e^{g_j/\tau}$. Its derivative with respect to $g_k$ is $-t_k/\tau + s_k/\tau$.
:::
